answer.exemplar: The field becomes one quarter as large, because field strength is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from a point charge.

questions.explanation: Inverse-square law means doubling distance quarters the field. The tempting idea is a simple inverse, halving instead.
questions.hint: Inverse square, not inverse.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Field of an infinite charged sheet
questions.learningObjective: Explain independence of sheet field from distance
questions.stem: In a chef's recipe costing sheet, explain why moving away from an infinite charged sheet does not weaken its field.

answer.exemplar: For an infinite sheet, Gauss's law over a pillbox gives a field determined only by surface charge density, so distance does not appear in the result.

questions.explanation: The pillbox argument yields E = sigma/(2 epsilon0), with no distance term. The tempting idea is point-charge fall-off.
questions.hint: No distance term appears in the result.

questions.topic: The electric field as force per unit charge
questions.learningObjective: Relate field to force on a charge
questions.stem: In a chef's recipe costing sheet, if the electric field doubles while charge stays fixed, what happens to the force on a test charge?

options.text: The force becomes zero
options.misconception: confuses field change with cancellation

options.text: The force halves
options.misconception: inverts the field-force proportionality

options.text: The force stays the same
options.misconception: ignores that force is charge times field

options.text: The force doubles

questions.explanation: Force on a charge is qE, so doubling E doubles F. The tempting ideas invert or ignore this proportionality.
questions.hint: F = qE, so force scales with field.

questions.stem: In a chef's recipe costing sheet, two equal charges produce fields of 100 N/C each at a point, pointing at 90 degrees; what is the net field magnitude?
